disease_label_per_paper: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection caused by Pseudomonas mendocina with Enterococcus faecalis co-isolate
presentation_summary: 70-year-old man with obstructive uropathy from benign prostatic hyperplasia and an indwelling Foley catheter presented to the emergency department with altered mental status.
He had tested positive for COVID-19 eight days earlier while living in an assisted living facility.
Past history included hypertension, recent hemorrhagic stroke, chronic kidney disease, encephalopathy, and dementia.
Initial labs showed leukocytosis and severe creatinine elevation; urinalysis was positive for leukocyte esterase, proteinuria, and hematuria.
Admission CT showed marked bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter with a bladder-lumen mass later understood as enlarged prostate tissue.
Urine cultures later grew Pseudomonas mendocina and Enterococcus faecalis; blood cultures were negative.

clinical_course: Empiric ceftriaxone was started and the Foley catheter was replaced while cultures were pending.
After cultures identified Pseudomonas mendocina and Enterococcus faecalis, therapy was changed to cefepime plus fosfomycin.
He completed inpatient cefepime/fosfomycin and was discharged with 7 days of outpatient ciprofloxacin, totaling 14 days of antibiotics.
Twelve days later he returned after traumatic Foley self-removal with anemia, altered mental status, AKI, and concern for UTI recurrence.
Readmission urine cultures were negative and antibiotics were stopped.
Ongoing catheter removal behavior led to bilateral nephrostomy tube placement and outpatient urology follow-up for definitive BPH/obstructive management.
actual_treatment: scheduled cefepime during readmission until cultures negative

outcome.source_text_value: initial UTI improved enough for discharge; later readmission required nephrostomy tubes and urology follow-up, with long-term status pending

quality_warnings: Pseudomonas mendocina and Enterococcus species, colony counts, susceptibilities, negative blood cultures, and treatment response are non-ranking confirmatory/treatment-context evidence.
Rankable evidence focuses on Foley catheter context, altered mental status, leukocytosis, renal dysfunction, urinalysis, and obstructive imaging.
